value: This article provides a comprehensive introduction to model theory, defining it as the study of interpreting any language (formal or natural) through set-theoretic structures, paradigmatically illustrated by Tarski's truth definition. It systematically introduces fundamental concepts such as interpretations, structures (which specify referents and domains), and model-theoretic truth. The text then explores how theories define classes of structures (axiomatization) and how formulas define relations within structures, highlighting model theory's formalization of common mathematical practices and its historical development. Furthermore, it delineates model-theoretic consequence, discusses the expressive strength of languages using techniques like Ehrenfeucht-Fraïssé games, and explains the application of nonstandard models in mathematical analysis. Finally, the article clarifies the distinction between a "model" in the technical sense and the broader concept of "modelling" a phenomenon, concluding with an overview of model theory's growing engagement with philosophical questions concerning reference, isomorphism, and the philosophy of mathematical practice.
